chapter_summary:
Having mastered the basics of Timeline, it's time to elevate your cinematics with more sophisticated camera work and visual polish. Manually animating camera keyframes can be precise but also rigid and time-consuming. This is where **Cinemachine**, Unity's procedural camera system, becomes indispensable. Cinemachine allows you to create intelligent virtual cameras that follow, track, and frame subjects automatically, and then orchestrate these cameras within Timeline for seamless cuts and blends.

To use Cinemachine with Timeline, you first need to install the Cinemachine package (Window -> Package Manager -> Unity Registry -> Cinemachine). Once installed, you'll typically have a **Cinemachine Brain** component on your main camera (if not, add it). The Cinemachine Brain is responsible for managing multiple virtual cameras and blending between them. In Timeline, you'll use a **Cinemachine Track** (or Camera Track) to control your virtual cameras.

To create a multi-shot cinematic:
1.  **Create Virtual Cameras:** In your scene, right-click -> Cinemachine -> Virtual Camera. Create several virtual cameras (`CM vcam1`, `CM vcam2`, etc.). Position and configure each virtual camera for a specific shot (e.g., `CM vcam1` for a wide shot, `CM vcam2` for a close-up on the character's face). Assign a "Follow" target (your character) and "Look At" target as needed.
2.  **Add Cinemachine Track to Timeline:** In your Timeline window, click the "+" button -> Cinemachine Track.
3.  **Place Virtual Camera Clips:** Drag your `CM vcam1` onto the Cinemachine Track. This creates a Cinemachine Shot clip. Extend it for the duration of your first shot. Then, drag `CM vcam2` onto the track, placing it after `CM vcam1` or overlapping for a blend. Timeline will automatically handle the blending between these virtual cameras, creating smooth transitions between shots. You can adjust the blend duration directly on the track.

This approach offers immense flexibility. You can tweak virtual camera properties (lens, noise, body, aim) directly in the Inspector, and Timeline will seamlessly integrate these procedural camera movements. You can even animate virtual camera properties on an Animation Track nested within a Cinemachine Shot, giving you precise control over specific aspects while still leveraging Cinemachine's intelligence.

Once your camera work is solid, the next step is adding visual polish with **Post-Processing**. Post-processing effects (like Bloom, Vignette, Color Grading, Depth of Field) are full-screen image effects applied after the scene has been rendered, dramatically enhancing the mood and visual fidelity of your cinematic. To use post-processing, you need to install the Post Processing package (Window -> Package Manager -> Unity Registry -> Post Processing).

The general workflow for post-processing involves:
1.  **Create a Post-Process Volume:** In your scene, right-click -> 3D Object -> Post-process Volume.
2.  **Configure Volume:** Set its "Is Global" property to true for scene-wide effects, or define a collider for local effects.
3.  **Create a Profile:** Create a new Post-Process Profile asset (right-click in Project window -> Create -> Post-process Profile). Assign this profile to your Post-process Volume.
4.  **Add Effects:** In the Post-process Volume's Inspector, click "Add effect..." and choose the effects you want (e.g., Bloom, Color Grading, Depth of Field). Configure their properties within the profile.
5.  **Enable Post-Processing on Camera:** Ensure your main camera has a `PostProcessLayer` component and its "Layer" property matches the layer of your Post-process Volume.

For cinematics, you often want to change post-processing effects over time (e.g., a sudden desaturation for a dramatic moment, or a depth of field rack focus). Timeline allows you to animate Post-Process Volume properties. You can add an **Animation Track** for your Post-process Volume GameObject and record keyframes for specific effect properties within its assigned profile. For even more granular control, you can use **Control Tracks** to activate/deactivate different Post-process Volumes at specific times, or even animate the `weight` property of a volume to blend effects in and out.

Common mistakes with Cinemachine include forgetting the Cinemachine Brain on the main camera, or not properly binding the virtual cameras to the Cinemachine Track. For Post-Processing, a frequent issue is forgetting the `PostProcessLayer` on the camera or having a layer mismatch, resulting in no effects appearing. Also, over-doing post-processing can make a scene look artificial; use effects judiciously to enhance, not overwhelm. Safety-wise, remember that post-processing can be performance-intensive, so optimize profiles for target platforms, especially for real-time cinematics.

screens.title: Advanced Timeline & Post-Processing for Cinematics
screens.subtitle: Using Cinemachine and Post-Processing to craft multi-shot, polished cinematics

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to combine Unity's Cinemachine virtual cameras with Timeline to create multi-shot cinematics, and how to add visual polish using the Post-Processing stack. We'll show you the essential components to install and configure, the typical workflow for building shots and blends, and how to animate full-screen effects like Bloom and Color Grading over time. This matters because procedural virtual cameras let you iterate quickly and maintain cinematic framing without hand-keying every camera transform, while animated post-processing adds mood and focus that sells the moment. A concrete example we'll return to is building a three-shot sequence: a wide establishing shot, a close-up on the character, and a tracking reveal, then animating bloom to emphasize a dramatic beat. Common pitfalls include forgetting the Cinemachine Brain on the main camera or missing the PostProcessLayer, and we'll show you how to avoid those. By the end you'll be able to orchestrate camera cuts, blends, and timed visual effects inside Timeline to make cinematics that feel intentional and perform well. Ready to explore the key topics and hands-on steps?

keyIdea.text: Combine Cinemachine virtual cameras in a Timeline to manage multi-shot blends, and animate Post-Process Volumes or Control Tracks to change visual effects over time.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide the lab steps you will follow. First, you will install and bind Cinemachine and create virtual cameras that follow and look at targets, so you can iterate camera framing without animating every transform. Second, you will learn to use the Cinemachine Brain and Cinemachine Track to orchestrate multiple virtual cameras and let Timeline blend between shots cleanly. Third, you will install and configure Unity's Post-Processing stack, create Post-Process Volumes and Profiles, and enable the PostProcessLayer on your camera so effects render correctly. Fourth, you will animate post-processing properties inside Timeline—either by keyframing properties on an Animation Track or by using Control Tracks to switch and blend volumes. Each objective includes a practical reason: these skills let you create cinematic pacing, emphasize dramatic beats, and keep your workflow non-destructive. A common misconception is that you must hand-key every camera; with Cinemachine you define behavior and let Timeline control when each vcam is active. These objectives will prepare you to build a multi-shot cinematic and animate visual effects efficiently and safely for performance.

screens.title: Cinemachine: Procedural Virtual Cameras
screens.subtitle: What a virtual camera is and why it replaces manual keyframing

narration.text: Cinemachine is Unity's procedural camera system that defines camera behavior through virtual cameras rather than explicit transform keyframes. A virtual camera encapsulates framing rules—such as what to follow, what to look at, lens settings, and body and aim behaviors—so the system computes the actual camera transform at runtime. The key advantage is iteration speed: instead of animating every camera position, you set up intelligent cameras that adapt to actor movement and environmental changes. For example, create a virtual camera named 'CloseUpShot' that sets a tight lens and assigns the character as both Follow and Look At. When the character moves, the virtual camera maintains framing without re-recording animation. A common misconception is that virtual cameras remove the need for all keyframing; that isn't true. Cinemachine is procedural but you can still nest animation tracks inside a Cinemachine Shot to animate lens properties or noise when you need a specific, timed change. Takeaway: think in terms of camera intent—what the shot should read—then let Cinemachine handle the technical motion details while you control timing in Timeline. Cinemachine: Procedural Virtual Cameras means a virtual camera is a cinemachine asset that defines behavior and framing rules, computed into a final camera transform at runtime.. In practical terms, what a virtual camera is and why it replaces manual keyframing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A virtual camera is a Cinemachine asset that defines behavior and framing rules, computed into a final camera transform at runtime.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Cinemachine: Procedural Virtual Cameras
What is a Virtual Camera?
A virtual camera stores framing rules: Follow, Look At, lens, body, and aim. Cinemachine computes the world camera from those rules.
Definition: An asset that defines camera behavior, not a rendered camera by itself.
Example: 'CloseUpShot' with Follow and Look At targets keeps the actor framed as they move.
Misconception: Cinemachine avoids all keyframes. In reality, nest animation when precise property control is required.
Visual: Virtual Camera Cards
CloseUpShot
Follow: Character | Look At: Head | Lens: 50mm | Body: Framing
WideShot
Static wide framing to establish environment scale
RevealShot
Configured to pan and follow for a reveal movement
Key Takeaway

Design shot intent with virtual cameras and use Timeline for timing and blends; add keyframed tweaks only where needed.

screens.title: Installing and Binding Cinemachine
screens.subtitle: Add the package, ensure Cinemachine Brain, create and bind virtual cameras

narration.text: The first practical step is installing Cinemachine, adding the Cinemachine Brain to your main camera, and creating virtual cameras that you can place into Timeline. Start by opening the Package Manager and installing Cinemachine from the Unity Registry. Then check the main camera in your scene: add the Cinemachine Brain component if it is not present. The Brain receives the outputs of active virtual cameras and blends between them. Next, create virtual cameras via the menu and name them semantically, for example 'WideShot', 'CloseUpShot', and 'RevealShot.' Configure Follow and Look At targets so the camera frames the actor consistently. In Timeline, add a Cinemachine Track and drag each virtual camera into the track to create Cinemachine Shot clips. Place clips sequentially and overlap slightly to create a blend. A concrete scenario: you want a close-up to begin at second five and overlap the wide shot for half a second to soften the cut; drag the CloseUpShot clip to start at five and overlap. A common mistake is forgetting to bind the virtual cameras to the Cinemachine Track; if clips show 'unbound', drag the vcam into the empty slot. Final question to reflect on: how does the Brain enable Timeline to control which virtual camera drives the main camera?

keyIdea.title: Install & Bind
keyIdea.text: Install Cinemachine, add Cinemachine Brain to the main camera, create virtual cameras, and place them as Cinemachine Shot clips on a Cinemachine Track.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Installing and Binding Cinemachine
Step-by-step
1. Open Package Manager → install Cinemachine.
2. Add Cinemachine Brain to the main Camera if missing.
3. Create vcams via GameObject → Cinemachine → Virtual Camera. Name them for shot intent.
4. In Timeline add a Cinemachine Track and drag each vcam into it to create Cinemachine Shot clips.
Practical Tip
If a clip is unbound in Timeline, drag its virtual camera into the clip's inspector slot to bind it. Naming vcams matters for readable timelines.
Visual: Timeline Shot Sequence
WideShot 0–5s
Establishing coverage
CloseUp 5–10s (overlap 0.5s)
Overlap to create a blend at cut
Reveal 10–end
Tracking reveal to finish the sequence
Key Takeaway

Install, bind, and sequence virtual cameras; small overlaps control blends and timing without manual interpolation.

screens.title: Cinemachine Brain & Tracks
screens.subtitle: How the Brain interacts with virtual cameras and Timeline

narration.text: The Cinemachine Brain is the runtime component on your main camera that listens to active virtual cameras and blends their outputs. Think of the Brain as the conductor: virtual cameras supply framing intent, and the Brain produces the final rendered camera transform. In Timeline, a Cinemachine Track feeds virtual camera clips to the Brain by activating Cinemachine Shot clips during playback. When two Cinemachine Shot clips overlap, Timeline requests a blend from the Brain for the overlap duration—this is how you get smooth transitions without manual crossfades. A concrete example: if WideShot runs to time 5 and CloseUpShot begins at 4.5, the Brain creates a half-second blend from the wide framing to the close-up framing. A common misconception is that the Brain automatically connects any camera; binding is required so Timeline knows which vcam each clip refers to. Also, you can nest an Animation Track under a Cinemachine Shot to animate lens or noise properties of that virtual camera while the Brain still manages blending. The takeaway is to treat the Brain as the single authority that composes virtual camera outputs into a unified camera—bind correctly and control blend lengths in Timeline for cinematic pacing.

keyIdea.title: Architecture
keyIdea.text: Cinemachine Brain on the main camera composes active virtual cameras into a final transform; Timeline's Cinemachine Track supplies which vcams are active and when.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Cinemachine Brain & Tracks
Role of the Brain
The Brain receives virtual camera outputs and blends them into the main camera transform during playback.
Bind vcams: ensure each Cinemachine Shot clip references the intended virtual camera.
Blend control: overlap clips to create a blend; adjust clip handles to set blend duration.
Nested control: add an Animation Track inside a Cinemachine Shot for properties like lens or noise.
Visual: Brain + Timeline
Cinemachine Brain
Composes active virtual cameras and blends during overlaps.
Cinemachine Track
Feeds Cinemachine Shot clips to the Brain for timeline-based control.
Key Takeaway

The Brain is the single composer of virtual cameras. Bind correctly and use clip overlaps for smooth cinematic transitions.

screens.title: Animating Virtual Camera Properties
screens.subtitle: When and how to keyframe lens, noise, and other vcam properties

narration.text: Although Cinemachine handles most camera motion procedurally, there are times when you want explicit control of a property: for example, ramping lens focal length for a push-in or adding noise during an explosion. To achieve this without breaking the Cinemachine workflow, add an Animation Track under the Cinemachine Shot clip and record keyframes for the virtual camera's exposed properties. This nested animation affects only that shot's vcam while Timeline still manages which vcam is active. A concrete example: you may want to animate the vcam's Field of View from 35 to 50 over two seconds to simulate a subtle push. Enter record mode on the Animation Track, scrub, and set the FOV keyframes at the start and end times. A common mistake is trying to animate the main camera instead of the virtual camera; animated changes on the main camera may be overwritten by the Brain. The closing insight is that nested animation gives you surgical control when Cinemachine's procedural rules need a temporary override or refinement—use it to enhance storytelling while preserving the benefits of virtual cameras. Animating Virtual Camera Properties means use an animation track nested in a cinemachine shot to keyframe virtual camera properties like fov or noise without disrupting procedural framing.. In practical terms, when and how to keyframe lens, noise, and other vcam properties. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Nested Animation
keyIdea.text: Use an Animation Track nested in a Cinemachine Shot to keyframe virtual camera properties like FOV or noise without disrupting procedural framing.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Animating Virtual Camera Properties
When to Animate a VCam
Use nested animation for lens changes, noise bursts, or other timed shifts that need precise keyframes while the Brain still blends shots.
Example Workflow
// Pseudo-steps (do this in Timeline)
1. Add an Animation Track under the Cinemachine Shot.
2. Click record and set FOV keyframes at start and end.
3. Stop record and scrub to confirm the animated property changes only during the shot.
Pro Tip

Animate the virtual camera, not the main camera. The Cinemachine Brain composes the final transform and will override main camera keyframes.

Visual: Nested Animation
FOV Ramp
Animate Field of View from 35 to 50 during a two-second push to simulate camera movement.
Noise Burst
Keyframe Noise amplitude for a short impact to add subtle shake without global animation.
Common Mistake

Animating the main camera instead of the virtual camera will be overwritten by the Brain; always animate the vcam exposed properties.

screens.title: Post-Processing: Volumes and Profiles
screens.subtitle: Set up a Post-Process Volume and a reusable Post-Process Profile

narration.text: Post-Processing applies full-screen image effects after rendering to create mood and cinematic quality. The typical workflow uses a Post-Process Volume GameObject and a Post-Process Profile asset. Create a Post-Process Volume in the scene and check 'Is Global' for scene-wide effects, or leave it local and use a collider for area-based application. Create a Post-Process Profile asset and assign it to the volume. Inside the profile you add effects such as Bloom, Vignette, Color Grading, and Depth of Field, and then tweak parameters like intensity, saturation, and focus distance. For example, a CinematicProfile might enable Bloom at a moderate intensity and add a subtle Vignette to draw the eye. Remember to add a PostProcessLayer to the main camera and set its Layer property so the camera samples the volume. A common issue is a layer mismatch, causing effects not to render. The key idea is to separate configuration (profiles) from placement (volumes) so you can reuse visual styles across scenes and control where they apply. Post-Processing: Volumes and Profiles means create a post-process volume, assign a post-process profile with selected effects, and enable postprocesslayer on the camera with matching layers.. In practical terms, set up a post-process volume and a reusable post-process profile. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Post-Processing Setup
keyIdea.text: Create a Post-Process Volume, assign a Post-Process Profile with selected effects, and enable PostProcessLayer on the camera with matching layers.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Post-Processing: Volumes and Profiles
Volume & Profile Workflow
Volumes define where effects apply; profiles store the effect settings you can reuse.
Create: Right-click → 3D Object → Post-process Volume. Check 'Is Global' for scene-wide use.
Profile: In Project, Create → Post-process Profile and assign it to the volume.
Camera: Add PostProcessLayer to the main camera and set the Layer property to match the volume.
Key Takeaway

Separate placement from configuration: volumes control where effects apply, profiles store consistent effect settings for reuse.

Visual: Profile Example
CinematicProfile
Bloom: 0.5 | Vignette: subtle | Color Grading: low contrast
LocalVolume
Collider-based volume for a camera tunnel or interior area
Common Mistake

If effects do not appear, check that the PostProcessLayer exists on the camera and that layer settings match the volume's layer.

screens.title: Animate Post-Processing in Timeline
screens.subtitle: Keyframe Bloom, Color Grading, or animate volume weight for blends

narration.text: Animating post-processing properties inside Timeline gives you time-based transitions that match camera beats. There are two common approaches: add an Animation Track for the Post-Process Volume GameObject and record keyframes for specific effect properties inside the assigned profile, or use a Control Track to activate and deactivate whole volumes and animate the volume's weight to blend effects. For example, to emphasize a dramatic reveal, you might animate Bloom intensity from 0 to 0.5 around the reveal, then back to 0. To do that, add an Animation Track for the PostProcessGlobal object, enter record mode, and set Bloom intensity keyframes at the desired times. Alternatively, create two volumes with different profiles and use a Control Track to trigger the second volume while animating its weight from 0 to 1 for a smooth transition. A common pitfall is animating the profile asset directly in a way that is not recorded on the GameObject; always animate the instantiated volume or its weight so Timeline serialization captures the change. The takeaway: choose between property keyframes or weight-based blending depending on whether you need targeted parameter changes or whole-profile swaps.

keyIdea.title: Animate Effects
keyIdea.text: Use Animation Tracks to keyframe effect properties or Control Tracks and volume weight to blend whole profiles over time.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Animate Post-Processing in Timeline
Two Approaches
Animation Track: Add for the Post-Process Volume GameObject and record property keyframes like Bloom intensity.
Control Track + Weight: Use Control Tracks to activate volumes and animate the volume's weight to blend profiles.
Example: Animate Bloom
// Steps
1. Add Animation Track for PostProcessGlobal.
2. Record Bloom intensity = 0 at start.
3. Record Bloom intensity = 0.5 at the dramatic beat.
4. Record Bloom intensity = 0 at the end.
Visual: Weight Blend
Volume A (Base)
Subtle color grading for base scene
Volume B (Dramatic)
High bloom & lower saturation
Key Takeaway

Animate properties for surgical control and animate weight to blend entire profiles; always animate the GameObject instance or weight for Timeline to serialize the change.

screens.title: Hands-on Lab: Create a Multi-Shot Cinematic
screens.subtitle: Step through building WideShot, CloseUp, Reveal, and animating bloom

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a multi-shot cinematic using the skills learned so far. Begin with your existing scene that contains a character and a basic Timeline. Install Cinemachine if needed. Create three virtual cameras and name them WideShot, CloseUpShot, and RevealShot. Position WideShot to cover the environment and extend it for the opening seconds. Position CloseUpShot to frame the character's face and set Follow and Look At on the character. Position RevealShot so it can pan from a prop to the character and set appropriate Body and Aim settings. In Timeline, remove any old Camera Animation Track, add a Cinemachine Track, and drag each vcam onto the track as Cinemachine Shot clips. Overlap CloseUp slightly with WideShot to create a blend, then overlap Reveal with CloseUp similarly. Next create a PostProcessVolume GameObject named PostProcessGlobal, check Is Global, and create a CinematicProfile with Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading settings. Add a PostProcessLayer to the main camera and set Layer to match. Finally, add an Animation Track to PostProcessGlobal and record Bloom intensity keyframes: zero at start, 0.5 mid, back to zero at end. Play the Timeline to verify camera blends and bloom animation. A common issue is forgetting to set the PostProcessLayer; if effects don't appear, check that first. This lab ties camera beats and visual transitions into a unified cinematic.

keyIdea.title: Lab Steps
keyIdea.text: Create three vcams, sequence them on a Cinemachine Track, set up a global Post-Process Volume and profile, and animate Bloom on an Animation Track to match camera beats.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Hands-on Lab: Multi-Shot Cinematic
Checklist
Prepare Scene: Ensure character and Timeline from previous chapter are present.
Create vcams: WideShot, CloseUpShot, RevealShot — set Follow/LookAt where needed.
Timeline: Add Cinemachine Track; drag vcams as Cinemachine Shot clips and overlap for blends.
Post-Processing: Create PostProcessGlobal volume, assign CinematicProfile with Bloom and Color Grading.
Animate: Add Animation Track to PostProcessGlobal and keyframe Bloom intensity across the timeline.
Quick Example: Bloom Keyframes
// Timeline keyframes for Bloom intensity
t = 0s  -> Bloom = 0.0
t = 6s  -> Bloom = 0.5 (dramatic beat)
t = 12s -> Bloom = 0.0
Checkpoint

Play the Timeline and confirm camera cuts and bloom animation happen in sync; if not, verify bindings and PostProcessLayer settings.

screens.title: Control Track vs Animation Track for Effects
screens.subtitle: Choosing when to keyframe properties vs. swapping/blending volumes

narration.text: When animating visual effects, you have two main Timeline strategies: use an Animation Track to keyframe property values on a Post-Process Volume instance, or use a Control Track to activate whole volumes and animate their weight. Use an Animation Track when you need targeted parameter control: for example, animating Bloom intensity, Color Grading saturation, or Depth of Field focus distance for specific moments. This gives precise, frame-level control. Use a Control Track when you want to swap or layer entire visual states—create separate volumes with different profiles and toggle them with the Control Track while animating weight to blend. A practical contrast: if you only need Bloom to swell, keyframe Bloom on an Animation Track. If you need to move from a gritty desaturated look to a vibrant filmic grade, layer two volumes and animate the weight of the top volume for a clean profile blend. Misconception to avoid: animating the project asset rather than the volume instance may not serialize correctly in Timeline. The takeaway: choose Animation Tracks for surgical adjustments and Control Tracks for state swaps and blended transitions.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Animation Tracks = direct property keyframes; Control Tracks = enable/disable volumes and animate weight for whole-profile transitions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Control Track vs Animation Track
Animation Track
Keyframe specific effect parameters on the Post-Process Volume instance.
Best for: Bloom ramps, DOF focus pulls, targeted color shifts.
Pros: Precise control, single-instance editing.
Cons: Manual keyframing for multiple properties.
Control Track + Weight
Activate or swap entire volumes, animating their weight to blend profiles.
Best for: Switching between distinct visual states or layering complete looks.
Pros: Quick swapping, clean profile management.
Cons: Less granular control over individual parameters unless profiles are built for it.
Key Takeaway

Match technique to the creative need: keyframe properties for surgical changes, weight-based volume blends for whole-look transitions.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Performance Considerations
screens.subtitle: What to check when camera blends or post-processing don't behave as expected

narration.text: Troubleshooting cinematics often comes down to a few recurring mistakes. First, check that the Cinemachine Brain is attached to the main camera; without it, virtual cameras won't drive the view. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Keep these core concepts in mind as you build cinematics. First, Cinemachine provides virtual cameras that encode framing rules; use Follow and Look At targets so shots adapt to movement. Second, the Cinemachine Brain on the main camera composes virtual camera outputs and blends automatically when Timeline overlaps Cinemachine Shot clips. Third, Post-Processing uses Volumes and Profiles to define visual styles, and the PostProcessLayer on the camera must match the volume layers for effects to render. These three ideas—virtual cameras, the Brain, and post-processing volumes—are the foundation for combining camera storytelling with visual polish. When you put them together in Timeline, you orchestrate both motion and mood. As a final reminder, animate the volume instance or weight in Timeline rather than editing profile assets directly so your changes are captured during playback and export.

narration.text: Before you move on, keep three concise reminders in mind. First, name and configure your virtual cameras for shot intent—clear naming makes Timeline work readable. Second, always check that the Cinemachine Brain and PostProcessLayer are present and that bindings and layer masks match; these small checks save a lot of debugging time. Third, prefer subtlety in post-processing: small, animated changes to Bloom or Color Grading often feel better than extreme settings. A quick practice: build the three-shot sequence, then try animating Bloom to punctuate just one narrative beat. Did the effect enhance the emotion or distract? That reflective check will help you choose the right intensity for final delivery.
